Q: Sort 'ls' output by name A:

The beauty of Unix-like tools is you can combine them:

ls -l | sort -k9,9

From the sort man page (man sort):

-k, --key=POS1[,POS2]
    start a key at POS1 (origin 1),
    end it at POS2 (default end
    of line)

POS is F[.C][OPTS], where F is the field number and C the character position in the field; both are origin 1. ...

OPTS is one or more single-letter ordering options, which override global ordering > options for that key. If no key is given, use the entire line as the key. ...

*** WARNING *** The locale specified by the environment affects sort order. Set LC_ALL=C to get the traditional sort order that uses native byte values.

The output of ls -l will look like this

-rw-rw-r-- 1 luckydonald luckydonald  532 Feb 21  2017 Makefile
-rwxrwxrwx 1 luckydonald luckydonald 4096 Nov 17 23:47 file.txt

So with 9,9 you sort column 9 up to the column 9, being the file names. You have to provide where to stop, which is the same column in this case. The columns start with 1.

Also, if you want to ignore upper/lower case, add --ignore-case to the sort command.

Q: Bash in vi-mode: browsing shell history with cursor up/down, cursor position not at the end? A:

So, for anyone still wondering, I consulted Claude and after a bit of trial and error I found the solution and Claude implemented it. Basically, I just put this in ~/.inputrc:

# Make it so when I scroll history the cursor ends up at the end of the line
# \C-p -> previous in history
# \C-n -> next in history
# $ -> press "$", the key to put yourself at the end of the line in vi mode
# set keymap vi-command -> set the following command when I press these keys in cmd mode, so "normal" mode
set keymap vi-command
"k": "\C-p$"
"j": "\C-n$"

As explained in my comments, this appends "$" when I scroll history, effectively making the cursor move at the end of the line

Q: How do you get the system default font size in Qt? A:

To acquire the current QApplication's font size, ::font provides pointSizeF and pixelSize. One of these shall return a useful value, whereas its counterparts shall return -1. If it returns -1, that means that the font was not defined via that method.

As an example, if the font is defined in pixels, it shall be available via pixelSize, but not pointSizeF, so pointSizeF shall return -1.

The current application's font size should be inherited from the OS, but if not, QFont font = QFontDatabase::systemFont(QFontDatabase::GeneralFont); should acquire it.

However, for sizing widgets (like one utilises "[r]em" and "[r]cap" for, in CSS), I have observed that QFontMetrics fm(QApplication::font());'s fm.descent();, fm.ascent();, and fm.height(); may be more useful, especially when the display scale is fractionally-scaled. I haven't confirmed this, though.

Q: If the reflection operator is applied to a conversion-function-id that corresponds to a conversion function template, what does its result represent? A:

GCC is incorrect. The experimental implementations of Clang and EDG are correct.

A reflect-expression has one of the following four forms: ^^::, ^^reflection-name, ^^type-id, ^^id-expression, where a reflection-name is a (possibly qualified) identifier. Since operator int is not an identifier, and it does not denote a type, the last interpretation (^^id-expression) is taken.

[expr.reflect]/7:

A reflect-expression R of the form ^^id-expression represents an entity determined as follows:

  • [...]
  • Otherwise, if the id-expression denotes an overload set S, overload resolution for the expression &S with no target shall select a unique function ([over.over]); R represents that function.
  • [...]

Here, &A::operator int denotes the unique function instantiated from the conversion function template. So ^^A::operator int represents that function.

Apparently, GCC fails to consider this scenario.
